segments.t: In the dining room, Vika meets with an affluent woman who wants to book a lavish birthday celebration. At first Vika assumes the banquet is for a two-year-old child named Tyomochka, until a tiny dog trots up to the table and reveals the truth.
Настя, принеси гостье чай или кофе.
Мне капучино без кофеина, пожалуйста.
И обязательно с безлактозным молоком.
И никакой корицы в чашке!
Значит, вы хотите отметить день рождения?
Да, моему Тёмочке исполняется два года.
То есть ваш банкет будет детским?
Почему вы думаете, что детский?
Он уже совсем взрослый мальчик.
А вот и мой хороший Тёма!
Познакомьтесь, пожалуйста, это мой Тёма.
Ты моя умница, иди ко мне.

'A decaf cappuccino for me, please.' the guest uses a polite everyday Russian courtesy expression that sets the tone of the conversation right away.

'And definitely with lactose-free milk.' the guest pairs 'definitely' with 'milk' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.

'And no cinnamon in the cup at all!' An emphatic negative determiner stresses her strict dietary rule.

'So, you want to celebrate a birthday?' In spoken Russian, the words stay in their normal statement order and Vika's rising voice at the end turns the line into a question.

'Yes, my little Tyoma is turning two years old.' In everyday Russian, 'turning' flows straight into 'years' without extra linking words.

'That is, your banquet will be for children?' In spoken Russian, the words stay in their normal statement order and Vika's rising voice at the end turns the line into a question.

'Why do you think it is for children?' The guest questions Vika's assumption with a subordinate clause.

'He is already a completely grown boy.' Here the guest anchors the thought on 'already' and finishes on 'boy', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.

'And here is my good boy Tyoma!' In everyday Russian, 'good' flows straight into 'tyoma' without extra linking words.
